title: Hospitality to guests
hookLine: the guest is honored; the door stays open

cards: Ji aayan nu. It's a Punjabi welcome, said at the door, sometimes with both hands pressed together, and a question follows close behind: tea? The kettle is already on.
A guest arrives, and the house rearranges itself around them. The good cup comes out. Someone gives up the best chair.
A small, ordinary scene, but in Sikh teaching it rests on something larger than manners. Yesterday was the meal. Today is the door, and the idea that it shouldn't be closed to anyone.

teach.h: SAANJHIVAAL: NO ONE IS AN OUTSIDER.
teach.b: First, the reason. In a hymn in Raag Majh, Guru Arjan says to God, in paraphrase, that all are called sharers in Your household, and You are seen as outside of no one.
The Punjabi word is saanjhivaal: partners, people who share. If God is within everyone, then no guest is a stranger. Second, the building.

teach.h: DOORS ON EVERY SIDE, TRADITION SAYS.
teach.b: The Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, the Golden Temple, is a place Sikhs hold dear, and tradition says its doors open on every side, as a sign that people from every direction are welcome.
Whatever you believe, whatever you're called, there's a way in from where you're standing. Third, what the gurdwara does with that.
Alongside the langar, some gurdwaras keep rooms where travelers can rest, and anyone can come in, cover their head, and sit.

teach.h: FOOD, SHADE, A PLACE ON THE FLOOR.
teach.b: The guest is honored with what the house has: food, shade, a place on the floor with everyone else. Fourth, the cost. An open door isn't always comfortable.
It lets in people who are loud, or sad, or not like us.

teach.h: WELCOME BEFORE YOU KNOW WHO KNOCKS.
teach.b: Keeping it open means deciding ahead of time that whoever knocks is welcome before you know who they are. That's hard when the doorbell rings and you're tired.
But it's what the hymn is pointing at: if God is outside of no one, the door has no one to close against.

how: Gurdwaras welcome anyone who comes, of any faith or none, asking that visitors cover their heads and remove their shoes; Sikh households traditionally greet guests with food and tea.

o: a formal etiquette for greeting elders
honoring every guest, since God is in everyone
welcoming only guests who share your faith

offer a head covering and show them in.
games.why: the door stays open: visitors are asked to cover their head and remove their shoes, then welcomed to sit and eat.

practice: Bring to mind someone who might come through your door, your inbox or your desk this week: a visitor, a new coworker, a neighbor you've only waved at.
Breathe in and see them arriving; breathe out and decide, before they get there, that they're welcome, with one small thing to offer: a drink, a chair, real attention, their name said properly.
If you pray, hold them in your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Hospitality to guests. The guest is honored because, as Guru Arjan sings, all are sharers, and God is outside of no one. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: saanjhivaal, sharers or partners, Guru Arjan's word for all people in one household.

carryVoice: Your line: the door stays open. Doors on every side, a way in from anywhere. Until tomorrow.
